rationale: Aitken, MATH 378 Ch.1, Axioms 1-4 give exactly this triple: N a set, 0 in N, sigma : N -> N; Axiom 2 'The image of sigma does not contain 0'; Axiom 3 'sigma is injective'; Axiom 4 (Induction) 'Suppose S is a subset of N such that (i) 0 in S and (ii) n in S implies sigma n in S. Then S = N.' Wikipedia axioms 1,6,7,8,9 (set form and predicate form) agree. The 0-based convention and the note that Peano's original started at 1 are both stated on the Wikipedia page. Definition only, no proof component.

Kaya, METU MATH 320, Definition 43: 'A set x is said to be inductive if (i) empty set in x and (ii) for all y (y in x -> S(y) in x)', with S(y)=y union {y} the same successor; Wikipedia Axiom of infinity states the same closure condition. The item's x^+ notation for y union {y} is notational only.

Kaya, METU MATH 320, section 4.1 constructs exactly this set by Separation inside an inductive set I supplied by the Axiom of Infinity: '{x in I : for all J (J is inductive -> x in J)} is a set ... A trivial but important observation is that N is inductive and that N is a subset of I for every inductive set I.' Delta: the item additionally asserts uniqueness of such a set, which the source leaves implicit; the item also names the set omega. The proof follows the source construction step for step, with the extensionality uniqueness argument added, so the proof is ai-altered rather than literature-derived.

Wikipedia set-theoretic definition of natural numbers: '0 = {} ... n+1 (the successor function) = n union {n}', N is 'the smallest set containing 0 and closed under the successor function', 'n = {0, 1, ..., n-1} for each natural number n'; Wikipedia Peano axioms, set-theoretic models: 'The set of natural numbers N is defined as the intersection of all sets closed under s that contain the empty set.' Definition only.

Kaya, METU MATH 320, Theorem 12 (The Principle of Induction) and its summary 'Any inductive subset of the set of natural numbers equals the set of natural numbers'; Wikipedia Peano axiom 9 gives both the set form ('If K is a set such that 0 is in K, and for every natural number n, n being in K implies that S(n) is in K, then K contains every natural number') and the predicate form, matching the item's two formulations exactly. The two-line proof (S is inductive, so omega is a subset of S, and S is a subset of N by hypothesis) is the source proof reworded.

Kaya, METU MATH 320, Definition 54 ('A set x is said to be transitive if every element of x is also a subset of x') and Exercise 32 ('Using induction, prove that n is transitive for all n in N'); irreflexivity of membership on naturals is the standard companion fact (the source derives asymmetry of the membership order from Foundation and notes Foundation is avoidable by induction). Delta: the item conjoins transitivity and n not in n into a single induction, which no located source states as one lemma; the simultaneous induction is locally written.

Wikipedia Peano axioms, set-theoretic models: 'The set N together with 0 and the successor function s : N -> N satisfies the Peano axioms.' UCR Math 144 notes: 'We can check directly that this set omega satisfies Peano Axioms, with sigma(x) = x union {x}'. Delta in the PROOF only: UCR proves injectivity using the Axiom of Foundation, the item instead uses transitivity and irreflexivity from lem-nat-transitive-irreflexive, a standard Foundation-free variant.

Aitken, MATH 378 Ch.1, Theorem 54 (Universal Property of N): 'Suppose A is a set, z in A is an element, and s : A -> A is a function. Then there is a unique function phi : N -> A such that phi(0) = z and phi o sigma = s o phi', proved from Axioms 1-4 alone, i.e. in an arbitrary Peano system, which is exactly the item's generality; Theorem 56 (Simple Recursion) restates it as g(0)=a, g(n+1)=f(g(n)). Kaya Theorem 14 gives the omega-only version. The item's proof is the same minimal-closed-subset-of-N x A argument as Aitken's z-closure proof, written out independently, hence ai-altered.

Kaya, METU MATH 320, section 4.2: 'It follows from the recursion theorem ... that for each m in N, there exists a (unique) function f_m : N -> N such that f_m(0) = m and f_m(S(n)) = S(f_m(n)) for all n in N ... and indeed is a binary operation from N^2 to N', with Lemma 15 (+(n,0)=n) and Lemma 16 (+(m,S(n))=S(+(m,n))); Aitken Theorem 4 and Lemma 5 with Remark 16 ('the above theorem and lemma are the two recursion conditions used in this approach'). Delta: the item merges the existence/uniqueness statement and the two recursion clauses into one corollary.

Wikipedia Peano axioms: 'a + 0 = a' and 'a + S(b) = S(a + b)'; Kaya writes the same as +(m,0)=m and +(m,S(n))=S(+(m,n)); Aitken Theorem 4 / Lemma 5 identical. Recursion on the second argument matches all three. Definition only.

Kaya, METU MATH 320, section 4.2: 'Using the recursion theorem, one can similarly prove that there exists a binary operation . on N such that m.0 = 0 and m.S(n) = (m.n) + m for all m, n in N'; Aitken Theorem 11 and Lemma 12 with Remark 20 name recursion as the alternative route. Delta: the item merges existence, uniqueness and the two clauses into one corollary and names the iterated map add_m.

Kaya, METU MATH 320: 'm . 0 = 0, m . S(n) = (m . n) + m'; UCR Math 144 (quoting Goldrei p.51): 'MULTIPLICATION n . k : n . 0 = 0 and n . sigma(k) = (n . k) + n'; Aitken Theorem 11 and Lemma 12 identical. Convention delta recorded: Wikipedia writes the second clause as a . S(b) = a + (a . b), the same product with the summands in the other order; the item follows the Kaya/Goldrei/Aitken order. Definition only.

Aitken, MATH 378 Ch.1, Exercise 11: 'Show that if n in N then n != sigma n. Do so by defining a certain set S subset of N and using the induction axiom to show S = N.' The item's statement and its proof strategy are both exactly this. Proof ai-altered: the source states the method but leaves the argument to the reader.

Aitken, MATH 378 Ch.1, Theorem 2: 'Every nonzero element of N has a predecessor in N', with Definition 3 defining 'a is a predecessor of b' as sigma a = b; Kaya Exercise 26: 'prove that for all n in N, we have that n = 0 or n = S(k) for some k in n'. Delta: Kaya's conclusion additionally gives k in n, which the item does not claim; Aitken's is the item's statement verbatim in predecessor language. The item's proof uses Aitken's exact device of putting 0 into S artificially.

Aitken, MATH 378 Ch.1, Lemma 8: 'If n in N then sigma^n(0) = n. In particular 0 + n = n'; Kaya Exercise 28: 'Using the principle of induction, show that 0 + n = n for all n in N'; Wikipedia Peano axioms: 'To prove commutativity of addition, first prove 0 + b = b'. The item's added observation that n + 0 = n is definitional is a restatement of the recursion clause.

Wikipedia Peano axioms: 'To prove commutativity of addition, first prove 0 + b = b and S(a) + b = S(a + b), each by induction on b' - the second is the item's statement verbatim, including the induction variable. Kaya Lemma 17 states the equivalent m + S(n) = S(m) + n; Aitken Lemma 9 gives the 1 + n = sigma n special case.

Aitken, MATH 378 Ch.1, Theorem 7 (Associative Law): 'For all x, y, z in N, x + (y + z) = (x + y) + z', proved by induction on z exactly as the item does; UCR Math 144 records the associative law of addition among the standard rules (Goldrei Theorem 3.12).

Aitken, MATH 378 Ch.1, Theorem 10 (Commutative Law): 'If x, y in N then x + y = y + x'; Kaya Lemma 18: 'For all m, n in N, m + n = n + m'. Both prove it by induction using the left-identity and left-successor lemmas, as the item does.

Aitken, MATH 378 Ch.1, Theorem 31 (Cancellation Law): 'Suppose x, y, z in N. Then x + z = y + z implies x = y'; Wikipedia Peano axioms records that (N, +) is a cancellative magma. Delta in the PROOF only: Aitken goes through the contrapositive Theorem 30, the item inducts on k directly using injectivity of sigma.

Aitken, MATH 378 Ch.1, Lemma 15 ('If n in N then 0 . n = 0'), Lemma 16 ('If n in N then 1 . n = n') and Theorem 13 ('For all m in N, m . 1 = m'); Wikipedia Peano axioms proves S(0) is both the right and the left multiplicative identity. Delta: the item bundles all three source results into one lemma, so the statement as a unit is a merge rather than an exact quotation.

Aitken, MATH 378 Ch.1, Corollary 18 (Distributive Law part 2): 'For all x, y, z in N, x(y + z) = xy + xz' - the item's left distributivity verbatim; Wikipedia Peano axioms states a . (b + c) = (a . b) + (a . c). Delta: the item additionally bundles the successor-left law sigma(a) . n = a . n + n, which is Aitken Theorem 14 ((x+y)z = xz + yz) specialised at y = 1 together with Lemma 16, but is not stated as such in any located source; the merge makes the unit ai-altered.

Aitken, MATH 378 Ch.1, Theorem 19 (Associative Law): 'For all x, y, z in N, x(yz) = (xy)z', proved by induction on the last variable using distributivity, exactly the item's route; UCR Math 144 records the associative law of multiplication (Goldrei Theorem 3.12).

Aitken, MATH 378 Ch.1, Theorem 17 (Commutative Law): 'For all x, y in N, xy = yx'; Wikipedia Peano axioms: 'it can be shown that multiplication is commutative and distributes over addition'. Aitken's proof is the same induction through sigma n . x = n . x + x that the item uses.

Aitken, MATH 378 Ch.1, Theorem 53: 'Suppose m, n in N. If mn = 0 then m = 0 or n = 0.' The item states this and its contrapositive. Delta in the PROOF only: Aitken derives it from the multiplicative cancellation law, the item proves the contrapositive directly from the recursion clauses and P1, which keeps the item ahead of lem-nat-mult-cancellative in the dependency order.

Wikipedia Peano axioms, Inequalities: 'For all a, b in N, a <= b if and only if there exists some c in N such that a + c = b' - the item's <= verbatim. Aitken Definition 11 (m < n iff there is a nonzero b with n = m + b), Definition 12 (m <= n iff m < n or m = n) and Theorem 34 (m <= n iff there exists b with n = m + b) show the item's derived strict order (m <= n and m != n) is equivalent to the source's primitive strict order; the convention delta is which of <, <= is taken as primitive. Definition only. NOTE for A2: the Remarks additionally assert that in the von Neumann model m <= n iff m is a subset of n and m < n iff m in n; that claim is true and standard (Kaya defines the order on omega by membership) but is nowhere proved on this page.

Aitken, MATH 378 Ch.1, Theorem 46 (Trichotomy): 'Suppose m, n in N. Then exactly one of the following can occur: (i) m < n, (ii) m = n, (iii) n < m'; Wikipedia Peano axioms: 'the ordering satisfies trichotomy'. Aitken's Lemmas 42-45 decompose the proof exactly as the item's steps 1.1, 1.2 (at most one) and 1.4, 2.1 (at least one) do.

Aitken, MATH 378 Ch.1, section 8 opens 'we will show that the order relations < and <= are linear orders' and supplies the pieces: Theorem 34 (reflexivity via b = 0), Corollary 36 (transitivity of <=), Exercise 49 (antisymmetry), Theorem 46 (totality); Wikipedia Peano axioms calls <= 'the usual total order relation'. Delta: no located source states the four properties of this additively defined <= as a single theorem, so the assembled statement is a merge.

Aitken, MATH 378 Ch.1, Theorem 48: 'Suppose that x, y, z in N. Then x < y if and only if x + z < y + z. Similarly, x <= y if and only if x + z <= y + z.' Both biconditionals, in both the weak and the strict form, are exactly the item's statement. Wikipedia Peano axioms states the forward direction only.

Aitken, MATH 378 Ch.1, Theorem 47 ('If x <= y then xz <= yz') and Theorem 49 ('Suppose that x, y, z in N where z > 0. If x < y then xz < yz'), with Theorem 39 ('n != 0 if and only if n > 0') identifying the item's k != 0 with the source's z > 0. Together these are exactly the item's two claims. Wikipedia Peano axioms states the weak form only.

Aitken, MATH 378 Ch.1, Theorem 41: 'Let n in N. There is no x in N such that n < x < n + 1' - the item's second sentence verbatim (with sigma n = n + 1, Aitken Theorem 6); Kaya Exercise 25: 'Prove that for all k, n in N, we have k < S(n) iff k <= n', the same discreteness fact in the membership order. Delta: the item's headline equivalence m < n iff sigma(m) <= n is not stated in that form by either source (Aitken proves the forward half inside Lemma 45, Case 1), so the statement as a unit is a reformulation.

Aitken, MATH 378 Ch.1, Theorem 52 (Cancellation Law for Multiplication): 'Suppose x, y, z in N. If xz = yz and z != 0 then x = y.' The item's statement is verbatim, and its proof is Aitken's proof (trichotomy plus strict monotonicity, Theorem 49) written out.

Wikipedia Well-ordering principle: 'every non-empty subset of the nonnegative integers contains a least element ... there exists an element of A which is less than, or equal to, any other element of A' - the item's statement including the 'least' convention; Kaya Theorem 13, final clause: 'Every non-empty subset of N has a least element with respect to <'. Proof ai-altered: the standard induction-on-the-complement argument, which Wikipedia runs through strong induction and Kaya leaves as an exercise.

Wikipedia Mathematical induction, Complete (strong) induction, describes exactly the item's base-free course-of-values form: 'this is unnecessary if one can prove P(m) (assuming P(n) for all lower n) for all m >= 0 ... the base case is subsumed by the case m = 0, where P(0) is proved with no other P(n) assumed'; Wikipedia Peano axioms and Well-ordering principle state the variant that carries an explicit base case. Delta: the located sources state the with-base form as the primary one, so the item's base-free statement is a reformulation. The derivation from well-ordering by minimal counterexample is the standard argument.

Wikipedia Peano axioms, Models: 'Dedekind proved ... that any two models of the Peano axioms (including the second-order induction axiom) are isomorphic. In particular, given two models (N_A, 0_A, S_A) and (N_B, 0_B, S_B) of the Peano axioms, there is a unique homomorphism f : N_A -> N_B satisfying f(0_A) = 0_B, f(S_A(n)) = S_B(f(n)) and it is a bijection.' This is the item's statement, quantifiers and uniqueness included. The proof (two recursion applications, both composites identified with the identity by induction) is Dedekind's standard argument written out.

Aitken, MATH 378 Ch.1, Definition 1 ('Define 1 as sigma 0. Define 2 as sigma 1') and Exercise 20 ('Use the above theorem to prove that 1 + 1 = 2'); Wikipedia Peano axioms works the same unfolding a + 1 = a + S(0) = S(a + 0) = S(a). Delta: the sources pose the claim and the technique, the particular three-step unfolding written here is the item's own. Not an invented mathematical claim.

Aitken, MATH 378 Ch.1, Exercise 21 ('Prove that 2 + 2 = 4') with Exercise 3 defining the numerals 3,...,9 by iterated sigma; Wikipedia Peano axioms unfolds a + 2 = S(S(a)) the same way. Delta: the two-fold unfolding written here is the item's own presentation of a posed textbook exercise. Not an invented mathematical claim.

The witness is the standard independence model for the induction axiom. Encyclopedia of Mathematics, Peano axioms: 'The independence of Peano's axioms is proved by exhibiting, for each axiom, a model for which the axiom considered is false, but for which all the other axioms are true ... for axiom 5, it is the set N union {-1}.' Wikipedia Peano axioms, Nonstandard models, describes the shape the item uses: a copy of the standard naturals followed by copies of the integers; Sutner (CMU) draws the same picture. Delta: the located sources use N union {-1} (EoM) or N followed by Q-many copies of Z (Wikipedia/Sutner); the item uses a single adjoined copy of Z. Recoverable restatement of an established independence model, not an invented construction.

Encyclopedia of Mathematics, Peano axioms, gives the independence model for the injectivity axiom explicitly: 'for axiom 4, it is the set {0, 1}, with S0 = S1 = 1'. The item's witness {0,1,2} with sigma(0)=1, sigma(1)=2, sigma(2)=2 is the same finite lasso one step longer, chosen so that the collapse sigma(2)=sigma(1) is visible away from 0. Delta: the source's model has two elements, the item's has three; the mathematical content (P1 and induction hold, injectivity fails) is identical. Recoverable restatement of an established independence model, not an invented construction.

Aitken, MATH 378 Ch.1, Informal Exercise 2: 'Describe three distinct subsets of N that are closed under sigma but that are not all of N. By the above remark, none of your examples can contain 0. This shows the importance of checking the base case since all of these satisfy (ii) but not (i) of Axiom 4.' The item's refuted claim and its witness N minus {0} are exactly this exercise. Delta: the source poses it as an exercise and does not name the particular witness. Recoverable restatement, not an invented construction.
